comments.text:
We need transistor (or 1mm^2) price equivalent chart... that's how you show how exactly NV is making their $$$.
Example : Let's say a full GB202 die can contain four (4) fully enabled GB206 dies : Meaning, NV get's to sell 4 GB206 card for the price of one GB202 (this is based on area used on wafer metric alone). 
Q : What is more profitable to make, a cheapest fully enabled GB206 die, or the most expensive GB202 card ?
In GB202 vs GB206 case : Fully enabled GB202 doesn't exists, but "next best thing" NV is selling is at 8000$ USD (2000$ for 5090).
Fully enabled GB206 cards costs at minimum 380$, so x4 = 1520$ (keep in mind, card manufacturer has to pay the same for both 8GB and 16GB version of 5060 Ti). Now, think about this : What is easier/cheaper for NV to make : A single almost fully working GB202 die (which BTW needs to be made regardless of card it's used on), or 4x fully working GB206s ?
When you compare this 4:1 ratio of GB206 ("mid range") vs. GB202 ("flagship/full die") in older generations, you will know how much NV is raking in those margins. Hope this could be covered eventually by you guys, Thank you :)

​​ @bingbongwingwong Efficiency at low duty cycle tends to increase, when the max power consumption goes up. Most gaming PCs are not running at 100% load all the time (which is when total efficiency will typically be optimal, or close to that). But at lower load, you end up with a huge amount of silicon under power for a low amount of used performance. Especially bad for this are modern "Desktops" that use all kinds of animations, transparency effects, and run the full GPU hardware even for basic things like scrolling a text document.

The other reason why efficiency is falling that way is, because performance demand basically always scales with available performance. I.e. if cards get faster a lot of the new software will be less optimized. Or for example users will enable higher rendering quality levels (which tend to require exponentially larger amounts of computation), use a higher screen resolution, etc. So yes, efficiency is definitely dropping.

With CPUs, the efficiency issue is far far worse though. Nowadays, most software is ridiculously inefficient. For example any common web browser will take at least 10-100x the resources that it should when you open a simple HTML website.

comments.text: No one should have to use DLSS or any other up-scaling bullshit, we should be getting just the raw performance instead, for the money being charged and especially with current and older games. And the thing that pisses me off even more is that die area and power have to be wasted for faking the frame rate funk instead of just using that die area and power to give us real performance in rasterization and/or ray tracing. Wasting die space for bullshit "Ai up-scalling" on gaming cards is unacceptable. While I have used DLSS and AMD FSR in Cyberpunk 2077 when I thought I needed it, on quality setting with the latest versions I can run of DLSS and FSR on my RTX 2080 Super, I really have to look for the artifacts, but they are there and its worse than the normal Cyberpunk AA artifacting. And going anything below quality in DLSS and FSR just makes things worse for very little gain in FPS. I will never understand companies' obsession with gimmicks. We in the gaming world just want better performance and great picture quality. Instead, we are getting gimmicks that seem to smear Vaseline on our monitors and ruin picture quality for "performance improvements" that can be had by lowering a few graphics settings, or by using the power from up-scaling to actually render the frames for real at full resolution. I do not know anyone that wants these bullshit "Ai" features, we just want better performance without sacrificing visual quality. I can not think of a single time in the past that ANYONE wanted worse picture quality from their graphics cards if it meant better performance. This right here is why I have been telling friends that are upgrading PCs or building new ones to buy used parts, and screw buying new from Nvidia, AMD or Intel right now. Current Intel cards do not have the best track record of working well with lower end processors in a devastating screw up there, AMD's performance without the gimmicks is middling at best, even when its better than the Nvidia counterpart, and Nvidia's own performance with or without the gimmicks is laughable at best for the prices, they can all get bent. My roommate was lucky enough to buy a RTX 4080 not long after release, its been great, and he has ZERO reason to want to upgrade from it. He uses ray tracing in exactly one title, Forza Horizon 5, because it defaulted to 2560x1440 Extreme settings on everything. He doesn't use ray tracing in Cyberpunk 2077, when he did turn it on and to max settings, the performance tanked and it looked like garbage from the boiling shadow edges and weirdness with stairs, and it was made WAY worse when any form of up-scaling was turned on, even at Quality for the respective up-scaling tech, and was even worse with lower quality settings. While up-scaling has gotten...."better",  its still faking the funk, it still steals power reserves and die area to fake the funk, and NO ONE in the industry asked for Ai up-scaling garbage. If I want better performance from a game, I am perfectly willing to adjust settings and/or resolution in the game to compromise where I see fit, I would prefer not to fake frames and/or up-scale from a lower resolution trying to run higher in-game settings at my native resolution. I can't believe now that I can not recommend a new graphics card just as I can't recommend new vehicles from any of the manufacturers. I never thought I would live to see the day when stupidity and laziness has truly taken over so many industries.

comments.text:
I'm going to keep this one short as I have a minor story that is related to this (at least I think it is)
Late last month I was searching up parts and comparisons so I could decide on what I wanted to buy to build my next pc and move on from this laptop I've had for a few years. I wanted to go AMD on my GPU because of the NVidia stuff lately, so I started googling comparisons for various low-price AMD GPUs against my 3050 mobile.
I had heard of the stellar reputation of the website that was top-ranked in the results, but I didn't expect the true depths of what I found when I clicked that link.
The GPUs I compared against mine were anywhere from 3.5x (7600xt) to 7x (9070xt) faster than what I currently had across basically every single category, but the conclusion was abysmal. I was recommended to keep my current GPU, a 45 watt tdp mobile chip with 4GB of vram running at 2000MHz boost, over buying even a mid-range card like the 9070xt, which has a 300 watt tdp with 16GB of vram running at 3000MHz boost.
But it gets worse! Somehow...
This website also made claims that the AMD GPU had a series of flaws in its design and drivers that made it worthless compared to my 3050. The flaws were all ones that have been happening to NVidia GPUs since the 50 series launched (stuttering, drivers not working, random performance drops, crashes, system errors, etc.)

Oh and also they decided to take a dig at tech channels like yours in one of the comparisons (the 9070xt vs 3050 mobile comparison specifically). They claimed you and the other channels like you discussing this stuff are "wealthy tech youtuber[s]" who "rarely play games".

Thanks mostly to being a viewer of this channel, I know that's all bull. But there are only 2.5 million people subbed to GN, vs the tens of millions of buyers who might end up on that site by googling comparisons to their current hardware when they look to upgrade. I feel like that particular site carries a fair bit of responsibility for why nvidia aren't losing much marketshare despite everything they've done. I could be wrong, though.

comments.text: Tom's hardware is one of the most evil and deliberately misleading publications/websites out there. They made an article on the Elbrus 8C CPUs (released in 2015) and said the performance of them when compared to high end Xeons from 2020 was "terrible" even though the Xeons were clocked more than twice as high, had 8 fewer cores (32 Elbrus cores in a 4CPU configuration versus two 20 core Xeons), were on a much more advanced manufacturing process (14nm instead of the 28nm that the Elbrus were stuck with), were on DDR4 RAM as opposed to DDR3 RAM, and they didn't even make it clear if the Elbrus chips were operating in binary translation mode (running code native to x86 instead of the Elbrus architecture) or running code natively. We weren't even told how much the Elbrus CPUs costed in comparison to the Xeons, nor were we told the power consumption. And you want to know how much slower? It was only 2 to 3 times as slow. The Elbrus CPUs had almost every disadvantage going for it and yet it was able to be half as fast as the Xeons. But I'm supposed to believe that the performance was "bad". No! The CPU architecture itself was clearly not at fault. Clock for clock it seems to have even been superior. But that's tom hardware for you, deceitful and politically or bribe motivated writers instead of technology motivated.

comments.text:
Steve=, I very much understand where you are coming from and generally agree with you, but I have to say @6:40 you are going a little off the rails.   What this chart really says is that the flagship cards have gotten way more out of hand - and it shows in their price.   A more honest number would be take say the 70 series cars as a "zero baseline" and compare relative to that.  The flagship cards are no more relevant than judging the car market by using price relative to a pigani or a gold crusted whatever.  They are effectively meaningless in the market unless you have piles of stupid sponsor or streaming money to pay for them,  Most people will not have one, and it ha been that way for 3 generations now.

 Similarly @8:00 I think it is a more honest way to say that as is common to most generational increases. the 5060ti is in the range of the previous generation 70 series cards.  Trust me when I say there are plenty of people out there who couldn't sell their car to buy a 4070fe if they could find one... but would be honestly thrilled to get a 5060ti that does more of less the same.  

As for the idea that NVidia is actively trying to deceive consumers, I don't disagree with you here either, however (the big but, if you like) They aren't lying.   They are showing the version of the truth which is best to sell their product.  Companies are not in any way obliged to write press releases that say "This product is 50% slower than the GPU you really wanted" or "this product is aimed at people with not enough money to buy our ransomware priced products".    I understand you hating on them 100%, but I think you need to find specific claims that are unfair or downright lies.  Shaded truth is what marketing is all about.    It is how Chevy sold the Vega or Ford sold the pinto.   They wrote the ad copy to tell you all the great thing about the car and didn't spend most of the page comparing it to a Cadillac or lincoln.  That is marketing.  Charts without scales and such are marketing.

As an example, let's say they are trying to run Cyberpunk or The Last of Us or some ray tracing only style title... whatever.  Maybe the 1050 can't manage more than say 2 or 3 FPS, and given that, if the 5050 at 1080p with all the bells and whistles gives you 150 fps (with many fake frames, of course) then yes, it is 60-70 times "better".    ia also think it seems quite direct that a 4060 and 5050 have a very similar baseline, but that the 5050 has better processing to generate them fake frames.

You might consider that it could well be performance at release, as an example.  You never know.

Nvidia is also correct in many ways:  A huge percentage of the "gamer" market are still running at best low end 2 series cards, most on things like the 1060s, RX580s, and the like.  For that big universe, a 5050 even with 8 gig would be a really big step up, especially in 1080p gaming world.   Yes, I know we aren't suppose to be going 1080p gaming any more, but for those players and there are a buck load of them, this is a huge step up.   Your own charts show it.   

YES, and this is important YES I THINK NVIDIA IS USING SHADY MARKETING TO BE LESS THAN DIRECT WITH CONSUMERS.   Every company selling any product in the world pretty much does the same thing, convincing you that this new model is better that that crappy old model they sold you last year.  it is the nature of marketing.

Given the likely use case (example, my son's computer has a rx580 in it...) this is most certainly one of the best price point NEW video cards, at least it seems.  It won't be great, it won't be amazing, and the 8GB means it will have a short life, but for 1080p gaming and the desire to get a better frame rate and some them nice traced things, this is where the game lands.

One more thing, and this is very important:  GPUs are at end game right now.  The technology is fairly played out at this point.  Much like buying a lambo or a ferrari, in most places you can't use the apparent speed for anything, and the actual use case of getting the groceries is better served by much more reasonable hardware.  80 and 90 series cards are mostly overkill now. The consumer need is not there, the visible advantage is beyond the realm of what consumers are likely to care about.  Oh, sure there are some who will always care, but most of the market is till on a 1060 or 1080... so yeah.   Something has to happen to make the consumer want what is next so much... and right now, there is not there.   The generational gains are not there, plain and simple. We are at (and possibly past) peak GPU in the classic sense.

comments.text:
Yeah, to go off of the end, it concerns me too. Nvidia is able to get away with this because they have a virtual monopoly. AMD is barely competing and intel struggles to penetrate into the market at all given the high costs of doing so. 


I consider myself a mainstream PC gamer. I'm part of that traditional "60" series crowd. Ya know, spend $200-300 on a GPU. The 50 series was always the more budget oriented gamer cards. They were okay but they were a bit on the lower end. I remember when nvidia made 10-40 series cards but those were terrible and were a literal waste of sand. 

Since Nvidia invented their RT line, they've lost touch with consumers. When Nvidia charged $350 for the RTX 2060 in 2018, I knew they went insane. The 16 series was a sad excuse of a joke and a way to give a finger to the entire bottom half of the market at the time. And then with the 30 series, they never replaced it. The $330 RTX 3060 was "it" for a while, and then COVID caused prices to go insane. Then they came out with the $250 3050 during the peak of COVID pricing and it seemed like they were doing us a favor, but let's face it, the 3050 was ALWAYS a waste of sand.

Especially since after COVID AMD's 6000 series cards got REAL cheap by comparison. And that's what I bought to replace my 1060. AMD wanted like $190-220 for a 6600 and $230-270 for a 6650 XT. Nvidia wanted $280 for an anemic 3050 and $340 for a 3060. Why the hell would I ever buy a 3060? If I was in the market that expensive, I'd want a 6700 XT which was $350 at the time. Either way, spending over $300 was way too much for me so I decided to get a $230 6650 XT and was done with it.

I'm glad nvidia finally came back to having $299 60 cards, but they still kinda suck for the money. THe 4060 was barely faster than my 6650 XT, and while the 5060 is better it's STILL pushing 8 GB in 2025. Of course, if i wanted more than anemic 8 GB today I'd need to...once again...go up to the $350ish range for a 9060 XT. Ugh. I just want to go back to $250 cards that were decent. This 5050 is a joke. I dont even see the point of it existing. Like, this should be $200 tops, and that's only in this current market. In reality, I miss when you could get decent 50 cards for $150ish. I just feel like the market is insane, and for all the people who scream BUT BUT INFLATION...uh...most inflation is greedflation and corporations are charging more simply because they feel like they can get away with it. The last thing we consumers should be doing is defending this crap. 

Anyway, I'm on team red for GPUs for now given nvidia's greed but even AMD isnt as cheap as it really should be IMO.

comments.text: AMD being a generation behind in ray tracing is one of the big instigators of this situation, plus not having rock solid drivers means they’ll only ever be player 2 just like they have been for years.  The only way a card with those two problems generally going for it is going to gain market share is by being a lot cheaper…which they aren’t.  Most people who are considering spending the kind of money for mid-upper tier cards don’t really want “almost”…. I want to play games and not haggle with janky drivers, and even if ray tracing isn’t at the forefront of my priority list, it is going to continue to become more prevalent, so would rather have something that is capable with it.  I would have considered AMD except that how far behind their ray tracing performance is kind of forced my hand.  ATi/AMD has always been like that ever since my first real graphics card (ATi Radeon 32MB aka Rage6).  They’ve always kind of played 2nd fiddle for one thing or another, except for the 9700/9800 glory days of course.  If it wasn’t drivers, it was fill rate, or power consumption, or inefficient architecture,  or just plain confusing marketing and product naming schedules (that actually makes a big difference for most of the people not intimately up to speed with every manufacturer’s entire product lineup…), and they just always struggled in one way or another with having a nice flat straightforward value equation unless you were a fanboy or a mid tier value conscious gamer who knew the tradeoffs and were good with them.  NVidia got that act together with the GeForce 6 series cards and I just haven’t been able to pull out of team green ever since.  I’ve had many used second hand cards over the years, so buying the good stuff a little later and much cheaper is absolutely a great strategy and has been forever.  Now it feels like either AMD will have to catch up on ray tracing and pull out another 9700 Pro level of home run, and/or nVidia will have to become so top heavy and self absorbed that they implode in some way as any of the other fallen greats have done over the years.  Another modern day rerun of 9800 Pro vs GeForce FX5800 would be awesome.

If this was a 75W GPU, it would be defensible. Even though it's expensive, the great efficiency and not having to use a PCIe power cable would be a great advantage, particularly because it makes it viable for upgrading office PCs with terrible PSUs. An i3-12100, Ryzen 5 5600G, i5-10500, or better, won't significantly bottleneck an RTX 5050, so the pairing would be a great value option for people who already had a computer and wanted to get into gaming - while $250 is a lot for a low-end GPU, it's still much cheaper than buying a whole new gaming PC.
But it's not 75W, so it isn't defensible. This is a terrible product which does not need to exist, and absolutely should not cost $250. It's the same price and doesn't have significantly better efficiency or performance than midrange GPUs from 2 generations ago. comments.text:
At the risk of being That Guy, I think you're being a little misleading yourself, Steve, when you show eBay pages of used GPUs.  That page you showed of an RTX 3080 10GB being available for $300.00 was, IMHO, misleading.  That's either the offered price, or the current high bid.

What you need to do is scroll down and select  "Completed Items" to see what prices they actually sold for.  In my very quick search as of this writing, RTX 3080 10GBs in working condition (i.e. not parts-only boards) are going for anywhere from $300 - $425, with most being in the range of $325 - $375.  That's not much more, but it is more.

The gap between offered and completed prices grows even wider with RTX 3080 Ti cards, frequently offering for $300 - $550, but most often selling for $400 - $650, with $450 - $600 being the most common.  And, as always on eBay, you have to pay attention to the shipping costs as well.

There are outliers, certainly, but searching on Completed Items will give you the most realistic picture of the current market for those items -- at least until eBay ruins it when they duct-tape an LLM on to the search system.

comments.text:
I was just thinking last night how boring hardware releases are these days. Questionably useful features that can massively degrade performance (Raytracing) and maybe a 10% performance improvement if you're lucky. Going back 20 years, T&L (Transform and Lighting) had recently made its way into GPUs offloading a bunch for computation from the CPU and majorly increasing performance. Multi sampling and super sampling were introduced, causing none of the blurred textures of modern AA methods and giving you much cleaner lines for a modest performance hit, at least compared to running at a higher resolution which would have been the only other way to clean up the line edges. People were coming up with crazy peripherals left and right, many of them questionably useful but cool nonetheless (3d mouse, an actual smellavision device, a force feedback mouse, an absolute plethora of joysticks many with precision force feedback... It was wild). 3d sound was a major focus with Aureal 3D battling Creative's EAX for positioning and environmental sound. When was the last time you saw a game highlight their audio in marketing? When when the last time the lights went out in a game, you heard something behind you, you turned and fired just based on the sound and when the lights came back up, there was a dead enemy feet from you? That happened to me in Unreal, and I'll remember how awesome that moment was forever. 3d Audio gave me that moment.

I guess what hardware is missing these days is the risks and the imagination. Instead of "let's throw everything at the wall and see what sticks" we just get "repeat whatever sold last gen, and I guess improve it a little if it isn't too much trouble."

​ @GamersNexus  Psssht ;)

Still your words hold absolute truth and power. Why buy a 200$ GPU if you get the same power for a CPU with iGPU. Since you are picking on the lowest possible end you surely wont pair a X3D with that GPU for playing - if you are doing just Excel eXtreme or whatever ridiculous workload, you can simply go with the iGPU of that X3D. Else I got a fine Gerald from Riva TNT here, that is enough to power your console.

So the iGPU is the absolute baseline of what a GPU should be able to deliver. A good point would be to go double or triple of that for the slowest stuff. And AMD isn't even trying in my opinion - at least with the 8xxxG. Why?
- No X3D to keep the CPU of the RAM interface - and that leads to stalls here and there if both want the RAM
- Why no on-PCB DDR-L4 buffer like the intel 5775C? You'd absolutely free up the DRAM interface on the GPU end imo
- Why do we have dual channel with dual dimms here? It's about time we go quad channel single dimm (so 4 dimms which are all accessed at the same time). Double speed, no more unused DIMM-slots. This also makes more sense if we go more and more cores and might be a good alternative to CAMM for now.
- iGPU creates heat. Yes. Most towers have a rather large cutout area behind the CPU. Use that for cooling. You can easily take of 5-10°C from 2 sources: your CPU and your VRMs. Thru-PCB conducting is possible and it is not optimized in any way yet. Still the sheer size of the area compared to thickness (socket, cpu-pcb and so on) should allow for cooling a reasonable 20%+ of heat the CPU generated
- 250$ still leaves a lot of room for ... more ... MOAR ...
- if I remember correctly the 8xxxG is a mix of Zen4C slower cores and Zen4 cores - and it has less of them.

Put all that together: less RAM interface usage by CPU -> more RAM interface for iGPU + doubled amount of channels + more heat put away --> more headroom for iGPU ==> more iGPU-cores
And while the 8700G is somewhere between 1060 and 1070 imo with +30% frequency, +300% cores and buffers + quad-chn we'll most likely see 1080Ti performance or with a tad of very well done maybe even 2080Ti. Which makes everything below a 5060Ti unnecessary. And thus resolves all the questions regarding low end systems in 1. And MAYBE that will trigger nGreedia to push up the % for units and shaders back to where they were and thus trigger a good development for all of us. Except nVidia - because everyone will see the nGreedia even more.

comments.text:
Binning has its place, but using it to basically scam consumers crosses a line that shouldn't be crossed by a reputable company. AMD for example, used it to great effect over the years with their CPUs, especially with Ryzen and working the kinks out of using a new fab process. Not only where they able to take advantage of binning based on useable chiplet core counts but also things like whether or not they met or exceeded specifications as well.

Another issue with NVIDIA is they have gone more of a route of pushing as much power as possible, hence the new smaller boards with massive blow through cooling solutions, as opposed to optimizing and increasing efficiency. AMD on the other hand, through redesigns and optimizations with RDNA 4, not to mention going with a new lithography and fab process, they have not only increased its GPU performance with the 9000 series, but also increased its yields as well. This has led to their having to fuse off cores to produce lower tier GPUs with this new process as opposed to binning GPUs like they have done previously, similar to what was done with the 5000 through 7000 series. They obviously still bin GPUs for things like board partners making over clocked cards for example and I am sure that some cards that failed spec for the 9070 class cards were binned as well but not nearly like before.

The card is not for me (I can afford better options), but people on a budget absolutely want these options, which are highly viable for 1080p gaming with the incredible software stack including DLSS. I think Nvidia is spot on in their spec for their early coverage – rather than having Steve rant about cuda cores, testing real games at budget resolutions with all the bells turned on is exactly the scenario where this card makes sense. The rant just seems completely uncalled for, except for the valid point that some Nvidia marketing is a bit loose with "performance" means. But to the low-end gamers, performance DOES mean FPS, and it doesn't matter much if it's raw hardware or excellent upscaling. It would be equally silly to bash the card for having too little VRAM. There are other cards with more, and this serves many use cases fine.

comments.text:
Steve, you are being irrational (and describing yourself as mad, which actually means insane rather than angry, coincidentally is consistent with that). First, you are upset with Nvidia for making products that they sell at price points you do not like. If they did not make a number of these products for those willing to buy them, you would not be complaining right now. If they had never made the GB202 die and instead had a product lineup that only used the GB203 due onward, your own % of flagship analysis would have been much more favorable to them, and it would have shown that the 30 series was an amazing value compared to others.

Nvidia’s costs are rising from generation to generation in excess of inflation, and being angry (what you actually were) with Nvidia for passing those onto consumers is not reasonable. Moore’s law is dead for both SRAM and IO logic scaling, yet Nvidia is paying ever growing amounts to TSMC per wafer for each node shrink. When there is no node shrink, they have to rely exclusively on a mix of architectural improvements and increased die area. The increased die area is disproportionately more expensive since the probability of a defect grows quadratically with die size, which makes things even more expensive to produce. The use of GDDR7 on most of the product stack also has increased costs for Nvidia. You do not see AMD or Intel using GDDR7.

As for the RTX 5050 being a waste of sand, that does not hold in perspective. The GTX 1070, which I am certain you considered to be good in its time, cost $379 new in 2016. 9 years later and the RTX 5050 delivers 10% better performance for $249, without even adjusting for inflation. It has the same amount of VRAM and it not only runs all of the same games around 10% faster on average (excluding 32-bit PhysX titles; the 10% was calculated from the techpowerup database), but it can also run them using upscaling (admittedly from sub1080p resolutions) and frame generation, for even higher performance. You would have liked to see it have more RAM and for it to have better performance in newer titles. RAM prices per GB have not been declining at the same rate as they had in the past. Also what do you expect Nvidia to do in its die area budget? Maybe if they dropped support for DisplayPort 2.1b and HDMI 2.1b such that they only supported the display outputs that the GTX 1070 supported, they could have put more performance into it, but then you would be faulting them for that.

The world has changed. We no longer have huge increases in capability from generation to generation from new process nodes. When there is a newer process, there is not much improvement and when there is not, there is even less Nvidia’s product line is a symptom of that. If this were a pure matter of greed on Nvidia’s part, which seems to be your view, then AMD and Intel could easily be eating their lunch by launching vastly superior products at vastly superior price points, yet they are not. From your reporting, it seems to me that you would have preferred it had Nvidia never made the 50 series and left everyone on the 40 series, since then you would not have seen anemic increases from the 40 series. I think when presented the choice of the 50 series being launched, or skipped, everyone would say that launching it was a good idea, even if only to improve what is available in the used market.

Additionally, I know that you are extremely critical of Nvidia for how they have done marketing for the 50 series, yet try to look at it from what is likely their marketing guy’s perspective. Due to factors completely external to the company, they have the least interesting product launch in a decade and must do marketing for it to have a job. What do you expect them to do? The same could be said about AMD and RDNA4.

What is hurting the PC gaming industry is not Nvidia, which has been trying to keep it alive, but a mix of economics and physics. Due to physics, it is no longer possible to get amazing improvements from generation to generation in the same price point. Due to economics, you cannot have companies sacrifice their margins to keep the party going a little longer. First, there is an opportunity cost that must be justified. Is spending time making and selling these things even a worthwhile thing to do? Without those margins, the answer would be a resounding no. Enterprise hardware has always had superior margins (closer to 90% versus 50% for consumer hardware), and unlike in the past, they have no end of enterprise purchases at the higher margins, such that even what they are offering in the consumer space is hard to justify producing. Every wafer used to make consumer GPUs is a wafer that is leaving money on the table. We should be thanking Nvidia for continuing to produce them, despite the impact to its balance sheet.

Finally, the reality that has made PC gaming stagnate without ever increasing amounts of money is not only going to continue, but worsen. Competition is not going to do much to change this either, since everyone is under the same stresses. That is reality, and Nvidia is by no means at fault for it. Don’t look at how well Nvidia is doing financially from high priced enterprise offerings and label the PC gaming situation as borne out of greed. That is just greed on your part.

comments.text:
issue with modern products, be it CPUs or GPUs is that to even be able to produce these, you have to rely on the limited supply of silicon chips.
These chips cannon be produced without investments nearing hundreds of billions over a decade of time (look at China, they been trying and they are not even close yet)
So instead of making the chips, they all went with the cheapest option of buying it from the leading producer which is TSMC. Some companies like Intel and Samsung can product some silicon that is high enough level to keep up but it is nowhere near being able to compete.
TSMC is investing hundreds of billions to increase production which increase by like 10-30% year on year, while demand nearly doubles.

So limited amount of highest end silicon is split up for all the different companies and products and the main focus becomes the product that can produce the highest amount of profit for the smallest amount of silicon.

An AI card can sell for x10 the price of a gaming GPU using same amount of silicon.

comments.text:
My dad used to be mad at me for not recommending him any new GPUs for his PC, which used to be my older, yet still good PC for anything but modern AAA on 1080p (i7-8086K, 1080Ti). One of his games just wasn't running properly and he thought that it was because his PC was that much slower compared to what's needed now.

One day, I was a bit fed up with that and decided to actually shop with him for one, and asked him what he wanted: a mid-tier GPU (specifically NVIDIA since he had a bad run with AMD before back on the old R5 days) that would run modern AAA games at at least 60 to 144 FPS in 1080p.

I then showed him the prices for each GPU that would be worth actually purchasing for his purposes. He was so appalled at the prices that he never ever bothered me about upgrading to this day. He just changed games because the game he was playing (Icarus) was just that badly optimized, and never bothered looking into buying a GPU for the next few years, but rather playing older but better optimized games.

Thanks NVIDIA for helping me convince my dad not to purchase your own products!

comments.text:
It's honestly frustrating to see tech YouTubers only now starting to criticize Nvidia with the RTX 5000 series — like this is some sudden revelation, and never said no in the past. Let’s be clear: Nvidia’s anti-consumer practices didn’t just start. The price hikes, product segmentation (like re-releasing the same GPU under a different name), gimped VRAM on purpose, artificial tiering, and treating gamers like cash cows — that’s been going on for years.

The truth? tech YouTubers are part of why we’re in this mess. For years, they played along. Every new GPU was hyped as a "game-changer," even when the performance gains were minimal or the pricing made no sense. Review after review came out with the same script. They normalized Nvidia’s behavior and helped shift consumer expectations.

Some were clearly more critical than others, but a lot of big names stayed silent or softened their takes. Why? Early review samples, access to exclusive events, sponsorships — it’s a cozy ecosystem. Criticizing Nvidia meant risking access, and very few were willing to bite the hand that feeds.

Now that Nvidia has finally pushed the envelope so far that even casual consumers are angry, it’s suddenly “safe” to speak out and even threatening to release recorded phonecalls.

So yeah, Nvidia deserves criticism — but let’s not pretend like tech media is innocent. They helped shape the landscape we're in. If they had called this out years ago, something like making review demands public, maybe things wouldn’t have gone this far.
